newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan plans major stock market reform by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Jordan plans major stock market reform by year-end.

text.p: Jordan plans to introduce a new securities law by year end which will radically reform its bourse to help it compete regionally for foreign funds, the stock market director said on Wednesday.

"The new securities law hopefully will be issued before the end of the year and will aim at enhancing the efficiency, transparency and the overall performance of the stock market, and encouraging foreign investment," said Umayya Toukan director general of the Amman Financial Market (AMF).

Toukan told Reuters the new law, the first major overhaul of the AMF since it was set up in 1978 would "transform the exchange radically" to enhance its regional competitiveness to attract foreign funds.
The law, part of Jordan's wider IMF-backed reforms, will loosen the state's grip over the bourse and encourage faster and clearer presentation of company results.
Foreign investors can buy Jordanian shares under the terms of a 1995 investment law which sets a ceiling of 49-percent foreign ownership for the 98 firms listed on Amman's official market.
However, foreign purchases have totalled only a few million dollars since the start of 1996.
"It will breathe new life into foreign investor interest after a painful lull," said Omar al-Masri, managing director of Atlas Investment Group, which deals with foreign funds.

The cash-squeezed market, battered by a high interest rate policy that has diverted funds to higher-yield instruments, has seen its market capitalisation drop nine percent to 2.9 billion dinars ($4.1 billion) at the end of July from 3.2 billion dinars at the start of 1996.
The securities law, drafted with World Bank assistance, restructures the AMF, which now combines the running of the stock market with a regulatory role.
It sets up a government watchdog, the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) to oversee two new private-sector bodies.

The first is the Amman Securities Exchange, which will run the market's daily operations under the guidance of the SEC. The second is the central depository body for settlement and clearing of stock, which will centralise and automate the current manual share settlement which involves cumbersome paperwork.
The exchange and the central depository body will both have boards of directors composed of licensed financial brokerage firms.
The SEC with wide ranging powers to regulate and supervise all trading of securities will license brokerage firms, Toukan said.
The new law also regulates Jordan's first mutual funds, with managers' accreditation falling under SEC jursdiction.
Toukan said the AMF will be helped by the Paris Bourse and the French stock market's central depository and clearing body SICOVAM to automate the stock market's operations within a year.
A tender to construct a purpose-built stock exchange is expected soon with a completion target within 18 months.
The law will eliminate loopholes in current disclosure rules by penalising companies which delay announcements.
"Transparency of the investment climate through compulsory full financial disclosures is provided along international accounting standards," Toukan said.
